name: TextExpander
tagline: Expand local text snippets from abbreviations with forms and simple variables

pricing.notes: Annual individual plan divided by 12; monthly billing is higher.

tiers.name: Individual
tiers.limits: Individual snippet expansion and syncing; public page states no numeric snippet cap.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: Shared snippets and administration; snippet activity history limited to 7 days.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom administration and security with usage-based active-user billing.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual advertised 20% lower); 30-day trial with no card
pricing.hiddenCosts: Enterprise bills by active-user usage rather than a fixed public seat price. VAT/GST and local-currency conversion through Paddle can raise the checkout total.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For TextExpander, expand local text snippets from abbreviations with forms and simple variables. The hard boundary is cross-platform apps, team libraries, sync, analytics, and enterprise administration, plus os integration polish and maintenance.
coreLoopDIY: Build one focused macOS utility that expands local text snippets from abbreviations with forms and simple variables, exposes keyboard-first controls, and stores settings locally.
requirements: only the permissions required by the selected feature
whatYouLose: cross-platform apps, team libraries, sync, analytics, and enterprise administration
commercial support and rapid compatibility fixes
ongoingBurden: permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for TextExpander because small utilities are technically reproducible, but customers pay for polish and immediate fixes when an OS update breaks a daily habit. The recurring cost buys permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Espanso
priorArt.desc: Active open-source cross-platform text expansion utility with system integration.

alternatives.name: Espanso
alternatives.desc: TextExpander's forms, variables, dates, and scripts are here; the snippet editor is a YAML file.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Raycast Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A fine free snippet expander, but forms and richer fill-ins are not really there.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Text Blaze
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free tier is a demo-sized snippet set; full forms and dynamic rules are paid.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Individual plan and a single-purpose local Mac app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for TextExpander in an empty repository.
Use Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit where necessary, SQLite, and the macOS Keychain; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build one focused macOS utility that expands local text snippets from abbreviations with forms and simple variables, exposes keyboard-first controls, and stores settings locally.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a menu-bar app with a searchable command window and global hotkey.
Implement only the primary feature and one settings screen instead of a plugin platform.
Request permissions just in time and explain why each is needed before opening System Settings.
Store configuration locally, support export or import, and never capture unrelated user content.
Add launch-at-login, update-check opt-in, diagnostics export, and a complete uninstall note.
Write unit tests for transformation logic and one UI test for the core keyboard workflow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a third-party extension marketplace.
Deliberately leave out cloud accounts and cross-device sync.
Deliberately leave out broad automation that executes untrusted scripts.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
